1:
Calvin begins by resetting the clock. He reads the opening verb as a pluperfect — the Lord had said — so that what this chapter relates preceded, in order of time, the prayer at the end of the last, and it was this message, astonishing and almost fatal, that stirred Moses to the confused and vehement request that he might be blotted out of the book of life. Ellicott keeps the order as it stands but allows an interval, taking the words as a continuation and explanation of what was said before, though probably spoken at another time, after Moses had once more come down to the plain at the mountain's base. Gill fixes the place rather than the hour, since the command to depart is addressed not to the summit where Moses stood but to the camp at the foot, where the people had lain encamped some while. Henry hears in that one word the whole weight of the sentence: Sinai was the place appointed for setting up the tabernacle and the solemn worship, and in bidding them depart before it was done God intimates that it should not be done there at all, which was very expressive of his displeasure.

Which angel is promised the voices agree upon, and each reaches it by a different road. Gill says it is not the Angel of his presence, the eternal Word and Son of God, but a created angel, citing Aben Ezra: God does not here say the Angel that was known, whose name was in him. Clarke argues it from the earlier promise, where the angel to be sent was one in whom the name of God should be, whereas here nothing particular is specified of him — and the next clause settles it, since I will not go up in the midst of thee shows the guide is not the angel in whom Jehovah's name was, which is how the people themselves understood it, and hence their mourning. Ellicott grants the word is ambiguous, since it might designate the Angel of the Covenant or a mere ordinary angel on a par with those set over the destinies of other nations, and makes the same clause decide it. Calvin puts it most sharply: elsewhere in this book the angel denoted God's own familiar presence and was used interchangeably with the name of God itself, whereas here he sends the angel in such a way as to separate himself from the people.

What was withdrawn, and what was not, is the substance of the message. Calvin holds that in bidding Moses depart with the people God utterly renounces the charge he had hitherto sustained, promising only that they shall attain the inheritance and not that he will preside over them and cherish them as a father does his children; he repudiates them, so that they may no longer count themselves his peculiar people, and he names his oath lest they accuse him of faithlessness — thus depriving them of the grace of adoption while still asserting the steadfastness of his covenant. Ellicott makes the same point from the other side, that Israel's misconduct could not annul the promises made to the patriarchs. Henry explains the refusal by the name God gives them, a stiff-necked people: he would have brought them under the yoke of his law and they would not bow, and God judges men by the temper of their minds, since we know what a man does but God knows what he is. That they are left with an angel rather than with God is not because an angel would prove more compassionate, but because affronts offered to an angel would not be so provoking as those offered to the divine Majesty itself — from which Henry draws the rule that the greater the privileges we enjoy, the greater our danger if we do not live up to them.
4:
Gill states the tidings plainly: God would withdraw his gracious presence and send an angel instead. Ellicott counts it something in the people's favour that they felt such news to be evil at all, since it is natural for sinful men to shrink from the near presence of God, as these very Israelites had shrunk from it a short while before at the mountain; they would probably still have feared too close a contact, and yet they were unwilling that God should cease to be the leader and guide of the host, setting a value on a presence which they felt an angel's would ill replace. What they did he takes to be public rather than private, since they not only grieved inwardly but made a national lamentation. Calvin calls the message a thunderbolt, since such a divorce is more fatal than innumerable deaths: it might seem delightful to be masters of a rich and fertile land, but all its delights turned insipid and its fruitfulness became like famine once they perceived they would be only fatted for the day of slaughter. God promised these people, he adds, what might attract them for a season, and denied them the one thing they should have desired, that he would be their God.

The ornaments laid aside are described from the customs of the country. Ellicott observes that Orientals of both sexes have always affected ornament, Herodotus reporting that the Persians who went into Greece with Xerxes wore collars and bracelets of gold and Xenophon that the Medes indulged the same taste, while in Egypt men of station wore collars, armlets and bracelets; for such a people to strip themselves was a great act of self-denial. Clarke notes that the Greek version supposes they laid aside their upper garments as well, rendering the command as put off your robes of glory and your ornaments, and thinks the translators would not have inserted a circumstance Moses is silent about unless the practice were familiar to them. He finds it alive still in Pitts's account of the pilgrimage to Mecca, where the pilgrims lay off their clothes for two white cotton wrappers and go like humble penitents until the skin is burnt from their backs. He adds the Jewish tradition that the people had borne the divine name inscribed upon a plate of gold as their choicest ornament, many having surrendered it to make the calf, so that they were reckoned naked and defenceless already.

Whether the command produced the mourning or followed it divides the readings. Ellicott would render the opening words not the Lord had said but the Lord said, holding that the message did not precede the repentance of the people but came after it. Calvin takes the other course and makes the later verse explain the earlier, so that the people did not wear their ornaments precisely because God had forbidden it when he enjoined them to mourn. Keil paraphrases the threat itself — if I go a moment in the midst of thee I destroy thee, that is, were I to go up for a single moment I should be compelled to destroy thee because of thine obduracy — and reads the closing note about Horeb as meaning that from that time forward they left off the ornaments they had worn and assumed the outward appearance of a perpetual penitence, entering formally into a penitential condition. Ellicott finds mercy in the withdrawal, since the people learnt from it why God kept his distance: it was lest they be consumed. Wesley reads the command as an invitation rather than a sentence — put thyself into the posture of a penitent, that the dispute may be determined in thy favour and mercy may rejoice against judgment — and hears in the stripping a holy revenge which the people took upon themselves for having given their ear-rings to make the calf.
7:
Calvin reads the removal as a formal act of separation: it was a sign of divorce between God and Israel that the sacred tent should be carried beyond the camp and set up at a distance, as though God were tired of his connection with them. He had promised as a special blessing that he would dwell in the midst of the people, and by departing elsewhere he declares them polluted; in a word, the removal of the tabernacle was like the breaking of the tables, for as by breaking those Moses dissolved the covenant, so by this he deprived the people for a time of God's company and presence. Henry says the same in his own terms, that it is a sign God is angry when he removes his sanctuary, since his ordinances are the fruits of his favour and the tokens of his presence — while we have them with us we have him with us. Wesley abridges the point to a line: it stood afar off to signify to them that they were unworthy of it.

Whose tent it was the voices dispute. Ellicott would render the phrase not the tabernacle but his tent, since the Hebrew article often carries the force of a possessive, and he notes that the Greek version and a long line of commentators read it so; the words that follow he takes as pitched it for himself, that is, for his own resort, and the name he gave it was borrowed by anticipation from the sanctuary not yet built, for which it was a temporary substitute. Clarke agrees, and adds from the Talmudists that the distance was two thousand cubits. Keil takes it for a dwelling of Moses raised into a temporary shrine only because the pillar of cloud settled upon it and Jehovah talked with him there, and rejects both the view that it was the sanctuary of the later chapters and the notion of Clericus and others that it was an older shrine inherited from the fathers. Gill leaves the question open between Moses' own tent and some place erected for worship before the great one was built, remarking only that it can hardly be thought the people had no place of worship at all for a year after coming out of Egypt.

Calvin will not have the private-tent reading at any price, and sets six arguments against it. The text does not say Moses took away his own tabernacle but uses the word simply and by way of eminence; he did not change his habitation but went out thither from time to time to worship or consult God; it would have been unlawful to give a private tent the sacred name God had bestowed on his sanctuary; God testified it was his own dwelling by manifesting his glory there; it would have been absurd for the people to seek God in that direction unless the place were holy; and the whole point of the removal was that Moses did not withdraw himself from the people but stayed among them, showing rather that God withdrew from a profane place, which made the act a kind of excommunication. Henry, whichever tent it was, fastens on what happened next as the first gleam of mercy: though the tabernacle was removed, every one disposed to seek the Lord was welcome to follow it, private persons as well as Moses being invited to apply to God as intercessors. When God designs mercy he stirs up prayer — he will be sought unto, and, thanks be to his name, he may be sought unto, and will not reject the intercession of the poorest. Ellicott makes the same observation of the arrangement itself, that though Moses had designed the tent for his own special use he allowed all Israel to make use of it too.
8:
Gill infers from the comings and goings that this was not the place Moses lived in, since having pitched it he did not stay there but went to and fro. Wesley, following Henry, reads the people's watching as a change of heart: they looked after him in token of their respect for the man they had lately slighted and of their dependence on his mediation, by which it appeared how full of concern they were about the issue. Ellicott takes their rising as a mark of respect and reverence, and explains the movement of the cloud, since during the encampment in the plain its ordinary station was the summit of the mount, and only at this season did it come down whenever Moses entered the temporary tent, ascending again when he quitted it. Clarke finds in that regularity an argument: the cloud descending at these times and at no others precluded the possibility of deception, being a full proof that the thing was miraculous and a pledge of the divine presence, for it lay beyond the power of human art to counterfeit such an appearance — and, he insists, all the people saw it. Wesley draws out what their worship at the tent doors confessed: their adoration of the divine majesty, their thankfulness for a token given for good, since had God been pleased to kill them he would not have shown them such things, and their concurrence with Moses in whatever he should promise on their behalf.

What it means that God spoke face to face is handled carefully by all of them. Gill takes it strictly — not by an angel but by himself in person, not by dream or vision but in real visible appearance, not in dark speeches but plainly, and not by a voice from heaven at a distance but mouth to mouth. Clarke denies the personal appearance and reads the phrase as the familiarity and confidence with which the divine Being treated his servant, speaking to him by articulate sounds in his own language though no shape or similitude was then to be seen; what he chiefly excludes is that these communications came by visions, dreams, inward inspirations or the mediation of angels. Ellicott grants that the phrase marks a privilege peculiar to Moses but confesses that what exactly the peculiarity consisted in is not apparent, though he allows that Isaiah and Ezekiel were perhaps equally favoured later. Calvin meets the obvious objection, that a few verses on Moses is told he cannot see God's face: the solution is easy, since although God revealed himself to him in a peculiar manner he never appeared in the fullness of his glory, but only so far as man's infirmity could endure it. The phrase carries an implied comparison, that no man was ever equal to Moses, and this magnifies the Law itself, its minister reporting what he had familiarly learnt so that no ambiguity might be suspected.

The last clause raises a small difficulty about Joshua. Clarke observes that he was certainly not a young man in the literal sense, being above fifty, and passes on Ainsworth's explanation that he was so called in respect of his service and not his years, since ministry usually falls to the younger sort and all servants are therefore called young men; Clarke himself wonders whether the word may mean one unmarried. Calvin turns the same fact into a comment on grace, since Joshua was of mature age and yet God passed over many old men to set the younger to keep his tabernacle; and from Joshua's not departing he gathers, incidentally, that Moses dwelt in the camp. Wesley explains the arrangement simply: Moses turned back into the camp to tell the people what hopes he had of bringing the business to a good issue, and because he meant to return speedily he left Joshua behind him there.
12:
Gill notes only that Moses had come back from the camp to the tent again, and Clarke fills in what had passed between: we may suppose that on quitting the tent he went to the people and gave them some general account of the conversation he had lately had with the Lord, then returned and began to plead. Henry calls him a humble and importunate supplicant for two very great favours, who as a prince has power with God and prevails for both, and a type of Christ the great intercessor, whom the Father heareth always — for the people had by their sin deserved wrath, and the turning away of that Moses had already obtained, but they had forfeited God's favourable presence besides, and it is the return of that he is now begging. So, Henry adds, by the intercession of Christ we obtain not only the removal of the curse but an assurance of the blessing. Wesley compresses the whole observation into a sentence and keeps the type.

The first plea is drawn from the commission itself. Henry gives it in Moses' own accent, and Wesley after him: Lord, it is thou thyself that employest me, and wilt thou not own me? I am in the way of my duty, and shall I not have thy presence with me in that way? Thou hast ordered me a great work, and yet left me at a loss how to go about it. From which Henry takes the rule that whom God calls out to any service he will be sure to furnish with the assistances it needs, and that those who sincerely endeavour to do their duty may in faith beg direction and strength for the doing of it. Calvin describes what Moses had actually lost, and why the loss was worth pleading over. Since the revolt God had promised no more than that he would give the land, and though he added that his angel should lead them, that was a temporary blessing of the kind he confers promiscuously on other nations too; whereas the angel who had gone before them until now was frequently called the God of hosts, so that Israel might perceive God to be present with them in a peculiar manner.

The complaint is therefore about a silence. Clarke states it plainly: God having said he would not go up with the people, Moses wished to know whom he would send, since nothing had been told him beyond the general word that an angel should go. Ellicott finds the earlier promises genuinely ambiguous — what is meant by mine angel and by an angel? is it the Angel of the earlier chapter or not, and if not, who is it? Calvin thinks the complaint well founded, since in speaking generally of an ordinary angel God had withdrawn that special Deliverer, the guardian of the people; and he observes what Moses does not ask for — not that Aaron be restored to him, nor that any companion be joined with him in so arduous a task, but only that he may be assured of the continuance of God's former favour. As the ground of his confidence in asking he adduces nothing but the promises of God, resting on no dignity of his own and alleging no duties performed by which he had merited such favour, but contenting himself with the brief request that God would cause the event to answer to his own words. Ellicott takes up the phrase Moses leans on: God had shown that he knew him by name at the burning bush, and probably again when he called to him out of the midst of the cloud, but the exact expression had not been used before, and it implies a very high degree of favour, since God knows by name only those whom he greatly regards.
13:
Gill observes that the opening clause is not a doubt but a foothold: Moses says if I have found grace in thy sight not as questioning whether he had, but as taking it for granted and arguing from it, improving his interest in it as he pleads. Wesley, in words Henry had used before him, explains why the plea had to be pitched that way. Whatever favour God had expressed towards the people they had forfeited the benefit of, and so Moses lays the whole stress of his request upon what God had said to him — Lord, if thou wilt do anything for me, do this for the people. So, both men add, our Lord Jesus in his intercession presents himself to the Father as one in whom he is always well pleased, and thereby obtains mercy for us with whom he is justly displeased. Yet Moses does not leave the people out of the account, but insinuates that they too, unworthy as they were, stood in some relation to God: consider that this nation is thy people, a people thou hast done great things for, redeemed to thyself and taken into covenant with thyself — Lord, they are thy own, do not leave them.

What he asks to be shown is read two ways. Clarke takes the way for a manner of government: let me know how thou wouldst have this people led up and ruled, since they are thy people and should be guided in thy own way. Ellicott takes it for an intention rather than a method — thy course, thy purpose — so that the request is, let me know whether thou really meanest to withdraw thyself from us and put a created being in thy place, or not. On the closing clause Ellicott notes that Moses is glancing back at what God had said in the previous chapter, and reminding him that Israel are not merely Moses' people but, in a higher sense, God's own, as God had himself acknowledged more than once.

The answer is short and its shortness is the difficulty. Ellicott points out that there is no with thee in the original at all, so that the promise is ambiguous: Moses could not tell whether it was a personal assurance given to himself or a renewal of the old engagement to go with the nation, and it is precisely because he could not tell that he presses for something more explicit in the verses following. Clarke renders the Hebrew literally as my faces shall go, and takes it for a promise of varied manifestation — I shall give thee tokens of my grace and goodness through the whole of thy journey, and shall vary my appearances for thee as thy necessities require. Calvin reads the same words as granting exactly what Moses had asked, since God affirms in one word that he will go before them as he was wont, which was a sure pledge of his presence in no ordinary manner; for though the whole world is governed by his providence, his face does not appear there so conspicuously as in his protection of the Church. He presses the point further than the others: since the same Angel who had before presided over the camp now resumes the charge of guiding the people, the eternal divinity of Christ is clearly proved from it, and my face shall go before is as much as to say, I will so go before thee that thou shalt truly perceive I am with thee, as if thou sawest my face set before thine eyes in a mirror. The rest that is promised with it he refers to the perseverance of God's grace and its final accomplishment.
15:
Wesley says Moses speaks here as one who dreaded the very thought of going forward without God's presence, and Clarke shows why the dread was reasonable. Rendering the Hebrew literally as if thy faces do not go, he observes that without supernatural assistance and a most particular providence Moses knew it would be impossible either to govern such a people or to support them in the desert. By what means the manifestations should come he answers out of Isaiah, where the Angel of his presence saved them — so that the goodness and mercy of God were to be shown through the Angel of the Covenant, which he notes is the interpretation the Jews themselves give of the place. Calvin reads the answer as an acceptance with a condition attached, since Moses takes what is granted while signifying that it would be better and more desirable for him to perish in the desert than to go a step further without the manifest token of God's presence.

The argument then turns on what would prove the favour. Wesley puts the question as Moses means it: wherein shall it be known to the nations that have their eyes upon us that I and thy people have found grace in thy sight, so as to be separated from all people upon earth? Is it not that thou goest with us? Nothing short of that can answer these characters. Calvin holds that the paternal favour with which God had embraced the people could not be known at all unless he remained among them, and warns against supposing that something different is indicated here from what was said just before, since in exactly the same sense God is said to go before his people and to dwell in the midst of them. The separation itself he traces to its root: the favour spoken of refers to their election and gratuitous adoption, and the separation is its fruit, Moses intending to restore the violated covenant to its original force — and this, after all, is our real happiness, to be set apart from the heathen nations as God's own property. Clarke gives the separation a plainer content: by such protection they would be saved from idolatry and preserved in the true worship, and so kept distinct from all the people of the earth, who at that time, the Jews alone excepted, were idolaters. Gill fixes the scene of the plea, at Sinai among the mountains.

The grant, when it comes, is unqualified. Ellicott marks the moment: at length the promise is given unambiguously and Moses is rewarded for his importunity, for God's people have found grace in his sight, he will go up with them and so distinguish them from all the people on the face of the earth — and now at last Moses is satisfied. Gill notes what the going up would look like, God accompanying them himself in that amazing and distinguished manner, in the pillar of cloud and fire. Calvin observes that nothing new is added here, the words being a repetition meant to remove all doubt, and that God declares himself induced by no reason but the gratuitous favour with which he had embraced Moses, so that the whole amounts to a renewal of the covenant, the people being consecrated again and recovering the sacerdotal kingdom. Wesley ends on the intercession: see the power of prayer, see the riches of God's goodness, and see in type the prevalency of Christ's intercession, which he ever lives to make for all who come to God by him — the ground of that prevalency lying purely in his own merit, because thou hast found grace in my sight. Clarke adds that both promises were remarkably fulfilled, God continuing miraculously with the people until he brought them into the land, and keeping them from that day to this a distinct and unmixed nation.
18:
Keil marks what prompted it: Moses was emboldened by the promise just granted, and now prayed to see God's glory. Wesley finds the boldness remarkable, since Moses had lately been in the mount and enjoyed as intimate communion with God as ever any man on this side heaven, and yet is still desiring a further acquaintance; the words themselves he renders as make me to see it, that is, make it some way visible and enable me to bear the sight — not that Moses thought the divine essence could be seen with bodily eyes, but having hitherto only heard a voice out of a pillar of cloud or fire, he desired some representation of the glory. Gill works through what is excluded before saying what is meant: not any visible lustre such as he had already seen, nor the glorious essence, which is invisible, nor the glory of the heavenly state, which he knew he could not see till he came thither, but some visible representation he had never yet been shown — perhaps the Angel of God's presence, who is called his face, in whom there is so bright a display of the divine perfections. Clarke supposes he desired to see what constitutes the peculiar glory of the divine nature as it stands in relation to man, which many take to mean God's eternal mercy in sending Christ.

Calvin alone holds that the request went too far. Thus far, he says, the desires of Moses had been confined within the limits of moderation and sobriety, but now he is carried beyond due bounds and longs for more than is lawful or expedient, as is plain from the repulse he meets. Calvin is careful about the motive — it was not the foolish curiosity that so often tickles men's minds, for Moses had no other design than to be animated to confidence, that he might go on more cheerfully with his charge — yet the desire itself was improper though its object was right. And he turns it upon the reader: if the vanity of our nature tempts us to investigate God's glory more deeply than is right, let the passage restrain us, since this is the rule of sound and profitable knowledge, to be content with the measure of revelation.

The answer both grants and limits. Calvin observes that God declares at the outset how far he has listened and then adds a restriction, so that the prayer is not rejected altogether but only so far as Moses was too eagerly set on beholding the perfection of the glory. Gill takes the goodness promised to be the substance of the glory, since the glory of the Lord lies in his goodness, seen in his works and in the methods of his providence, but chiefly in the distribution of sovereign grace and most of all in pardon — for if it is the glory of a man to pass over a transgression, much more is it the glory of God. Clarke reads the same limitation as a mercy: thou shalt not have a sight of my justice, for thou couldst not bear the infinite splendour of my purity, but I shall show myself as the fountain of inexhaustible compassion, the sovereign Dispenser of my own mercy in my own way. Ellicott confesses it is not clear how the promise was fulfilled, and of the clause about grace cautions that it does not mean God's favour is bestowed arbitrarily, only that in any case it is favour, a free gift, neither earned nor merited. Calvin ends on where the weight of the revelation lay: though a vision was exhibited to the eyes, the main point was in the voice, since true acquaintance with God is made more by the ears than by the eyes, and speechless visions would be cold and evanescent did they not borrow their efficacy from words.
20:
Why the face cannot be seen each answers in his own idiom. Gill distinguishes what Moses must have known was impossible, the sight of the divine essence, from what was actually refused him, the fullest discoveries of God's grace in Christ, which are too much for a man who sees in part and through a glass darkly. Clarke says the splendour would be insufferable, since he only whose mortality is swallowed up of life can see God as he is. Calvin sets the refusal against what had already been granted: Jacob long before had said that he had seen God face to face, and Moses had received a clearer vision still, yet even now he obtains no perfect sight of God as he is in himself. Even the angels, said to see God's face more excellently than men, do not apprehend the immense perfection of his glory, by which they would be absorbed; and so God, while withholding complete knowledge, manifests himself as far as is expedient, attempering the light to our capacity and assuming the face we are able to bear.

The place appointed is described with more confidence than it can be located. Clarke takes it for a well-known spot where God had been accustomed to meet Moses, a rock with a cleft in it; Ellicott agrees a place on the summit is intended but holds it impossible to fix, and dismisses the speculations of travellers as of little value. Wesley reads the cleft as shelter from the dazzling light and devouring fire of the glory, and identifies it with the rock in Horeb from which the water was brought, of which it is said that the rock was Christ: in the clefts of that rock, he says, we are secured from the wrath which would otherwise consume us. Calvin allows that the whole description may appear puerile, and answers that it is well adapted to our imperfection. His figure for it is exact: the fissure in the rock was like a narrow and oblique window, admitting the sun's rays so far that a man shut up in a deep place gets some advantage from the light, yet never sees the sun itself nor enjoys its brightness.

What was seen, then, was a back and not a face. Wesley explains the image from human custom, since the face is the seat of majesty and men are known by their faces, whereas this was such a sight as we have of a man gone past us; and he notes that when Moses was afterwards witness to the transfiguration he saw that face shine as the sun. Gill reads the covering hand and its removal as two dispensations, the hand signifying the obscurity of the former and its withdrawal a clearer revelation of the grace of God in Christ. Calvin rejects one reading firmly, that the back parts mean the fullness of time when Christ was manifested in the flesh — a subtle speculation, but altogether wide of the genuine meaning — holding rather that we, imprisoned in our bodies, cannot behold God's glory directly, but are illuminated obliquely, so that at best we see him from behind. Ellicott ends on the limits of language: the mysteriousness of this section attains its highest climax in the last three verses, and human speech is by its nature unfit to express such truths, clothing them of necessity in a materialistic garment alien to them. All that can legitimately be gathered is that Moses was set in a retired position where God both protected and shrouded him while a manifestation of transcendent character passed by, and that he saw not the manifestation itself but the sort of after-glow it left behind, which was as much as human nature could endure. Clarke adds only that on some occasions to be kept in the dark is as instructive as to be brought into the light.
